summary: The note argues that urban gardens, from backyard patches to community parks, serve as vital biodiversity hotspots as urban sprawl shrinks natural habitats. It reviews research and expert comments on pollinators, birds, mammals, reptiles and amphibians, and notes threats from pesticides and domestic cats. It closes by calling for community action such as the "Wild in the City" initiative and innovative designs like vertical gardens and roof habitats.
one_line: Urban gardens act as crucial refuges for pollinators, birds, mammals, reptiles and amphibians amid urban sprawl, though pesticides and pets threaten them.
key_facts: Dr. Helen Torres, an urban ecologist from the Metropolitan University, presented findings on September 14, 2023 on accelerated loss of native wildlife habitats due to urban development.
Torres's research found that urban sprawl has doubled in the past two decades.
The Urban Wildlife Institute released a study on October 5, 2023 describing urban gardens as lifelines for urban-dwelling species.
Roberta Clarkson, a landscape architect and sustainable urban design advocate, suggests urban gardens can form wildlife corridors linking larger parks and reserves.
Beekeeper Simon Petrie said on November 3, 2023 that "Just one small garden can house thousands of pollinators."
Ornithologist Laura Chen said on December 1, 2023 that over 150 species have been documented using urban green spaces throughout the year.
Laura Chen stresses preserving native plant species in gardens because they offer the best nutrition and habitat for local birds.
A field study led by urban mammologist James Walters, published January 20, 2024, found green spaces are essential for city mammals such as squirrels, opossums and raccoons.
Herpetologist Maria Gomez reported on February 17, 2024 that city parks often host frog, lizard and snake species.
The City Wildlife Protection Agency released a report on March 8, 2024 urging residents and landscapers to minimize chemical use and use natural alternatives to pesticides.
Domestic pets, particularly cats, threaten urban wildlife; keeping cats indoors or in enclosed 'catios' is recommended.
The "Wild in the City" initiative was launched on April 5, 2024 to engage communities through events and educational programs.
Vertical gardens and roof habitats are being explored as ways to expand urban wildlife habitat.
